old: כאשר רופא מומחה במוסד קבע שמטופל בגיר אינו מסוגל להבין בענייניו הרפואיים ונזקק לטיפול שיש דחיפות לתיתו (ושאינו אשפוז פסיכיאטרי) (§14א(א)), ואין לו מיופה כוח או אפוטרופוס לענייניו הרפואיים — עובד סוציאלי במוסד הרפואי, באישור מנהל המוסד (בקופת חולים — הרופא המחוזי), רשאי לתת לבן משפחה בגיר אישור בכתב לשמש "מקבל החלטות זמני" (§14א(ב)).
new: כאשר רופא מומחה במוסד קבע שמטופל בגיר אינו מסוגל להבין בענייניו הרפואיים ונזקק לטיפול שיש דחיפות לתיתו (ושאינו אשפוז פסיכיאטרי) (§14א(א)), ואין לו מיופה כוח או אפוטרופוס לענייניו הרפואיים — עובד סוציאלי במוסד הרפואי, באישור מנהל המוסד (בקופת חולים — הרופא המחוזי), רשאי לתת לאדם בגיר אישור בכתב לשמש "מקבל החלטות זמני", לפי סדר הקדימויות שבסעיף 14ב ובכפוף לחריג שבסעיף 14ב(ה) למי ששמו נקוב בייפוי כוח שטרם נכנס לתוקף או בהנחיות מקדימות, בתנאי שיפעל לטובת המטופל, נתן הסכמה והצהרה בכתב והמטופל לא הביע התנגדות לאישורו (§14א(ב)(4)–(6)).

old: מקבל החלטות זמני (§14א): כאשר רופא מומחה קבע שמטופל בגיר אינו מסוגל להבין בענייניו הרפואיים וזקוק לטיפול דחוף (לא אשפוז פסיכיאטרי), ואין לו מיופה כוח/אפוטרופוס רפואי — עובד סוציאלי במוסד, באישור מנהל המוסד, יכול לאשר בן משפחה כמקבל החלטות זמני, לתוקף 6 חודשים מיום שניתן.
new: מקבל החלטות זמני (§14א): כאשר רופא מומחה קבע שמטופל בגיר אינו מסוגל להבין בענייניו הרפואיים וזקוק לטיפול דחוף (לא אשפוז פסיכיאטרי), ואין לו מיופה כוח/אפוטרופוס רפואי — עובד סוציאלי במוסד, באישור מנהל המוסד, יכול לאשר אדם בגיר כמקבל החלטות זמני לפי סדר הקדימויות בסעיף 14ב ובכפוף לחריג בסעיף 14ב(ה) למי ששמו נקוב בייפוי כוח שטרם נכנס לתוקף או בהנחיות מקדימות, בתנאי שיפעל לטובת המטופל, נתן הסכמה והצהרה בכתב והמטופל לא הביע התנגדות לאישורו (§14א(ב)(4)–(6)), לתוקף 6 חודשים מיום שניתן.

old: מקבל החלטות זמני — בן משפחה בגיר שמאושר בכתב על ידי עובד סוציאלי במוסד הרפואי (באישור מנהל המוסד), לאחר שרופא מומחה קבע שהמטופל אינו מסוגל להבין וזקוק לטיפול דחוף, לפי סדר הקדימויות (§14א-ב).
new: מקבל החלטות זמני — אדם בגיר שמאושר בכתב על ידי עובד סוציאלי במוסד הרפואי (באישור מנהל המוסד), לאחר שרופא מומחה קבע שהמטופל אינו מסוגל להבין וזקוק לטיפול דחוף, לפי סדר הקדימויות בסעיף 14ב ובכפוף לחריג בסעיף 14ב(ה) למי ששמו נקוב בייפוי כוח שטרם נכנס לתוקף או בהנחיות מקדימות, בתנאי שיפעל לטובת המטופל, נתן הסכמה והצהרה בכתב והמטופל לא הביע התנגדות לאישורו (§14א(ב)(4)–(6)).

old: Environmental: extrinsic factors contribute to 35–45% of injurious falls; 1/4 to 1/2 of falls occur away from home; a stairs fall carries ~2x the injury risk of other falls (p636–637).
new: Environmental: it has been estimated that extrinsic factors are involved in 35–45% of injurious falls; 1/4 to 1/2 of falls occur away from home; a stairs fall carries ~2x the injury risk of other falls (p636–637).

old: TUG test: rise from chair, walk 3 meters, turn, return, sit; a 25-study systematic review found limited predictive value and no validated cut-point (p637).
new: TUG test: rise from chair, walk 3 meters, turn, return, sit; a 25-study systematic review found limited predictive value in community-dwelling older adults and no cut-point for impaired performance could be recommended (p637).

old: Vision: first-eye cataract surgery → 34% fewer falls; second-eye surgery similar (~32%) but not statistically significant; keep post-op spectacle power change < ±0.75 diopter (p639). Updating glasses to correct prescription: evidence less clear — one RCT found no significant reduction, and another (vision assessment + treatment) increased falls by ~50% (p639). Single-lens distance glasses for habitual multifocal wearers: 40% fewer falls in the outdoor-active subgroup (p639). Home-safety modification for severe uncorrectable low vision: 41% fewer falls (p639).
new: Vision: first-eye cataract surgery → 34% fewer falls; second-eye surgery similar (~32%) but not statistically significant; one prospective cohort study associated cataract surgery with fewer falls provided post-op spectacle lens power updates were cautious (less than ±0.75 diopter change) (p639). Updating glasses to correct prescription: evidence less clear — one RCT found no significant reduction, and another (vision assessment + treatment) increased falls by ~50% (p639). Single-lens distance glasses for habitual multifocal wearers: 40% fewer falls in the outdoor-active subgroup (p639). Home-safety modification for severe uncorrectable low vision: 41% fewer falls (p639).

old: CSA is two to three times more prevalent at age 65–90 vs 39–64; upwards of 50% of stable heart-failure patients have some form of SDB (p646).
new: CSA is two to three times more prevalent at age 65–90 vs 39–64; an estimated upwards of 50% of stable heart-failure patients have some form of SDB (p646).

old: CPAP pressure usually 5 to 20 cm H2O; well tolerated above age 80 and in mild-moderate dementia (p649).
new: CPAP pressure usually 5 to 20 cm H2O; observational studies found it well tolerated above age 80 and in mild-moderate dementia (p649).

old: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation trials limited to BMI less than 32 kg/m2; cohort of 62 patients aged 65–80 showed benefit (p650).
new: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation trials limited to highly selected CPAP-intolerant patients with BMI less than 32 kg/m2; cohort of 62 patients aged 65–80 showed benefit (p650).

old: Start iron if ferritin less than 75 mcg/L; consider IV iron if ferritin less than 300 mcg/L with moderate-severe symptoms (p652).
new: Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in clinically significant RLS. AASM guidance considers iron at ferritin ≤75 µg/L or transferrin saturation <20%, with IV iron when ferritin is 75–100 µg/L if iron is indicated. The moderate–severe RLS trial permitting ferritin 75–300 µg/L required transferrin saturation <20% in that range (p652; trial, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).

old: A third of older patients had persistent severe insomnia at 4-year follow-up; more than 80% of women over 85 report sleeping difficulties (p658).
new: In one study, a third of older patients had persistent severe insomnia at 4-year follow-up; more than 80% of women over 85 report sleeping difficulties (p658).

old: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects, less amnestic (p660). Suvorexant/lemborexant (DORA) — only suvorexant FDA-approved for insomnia with Alzheimer dementia (trial of 277 patients, mild-moderate AD, sleep time up around half an hour after 2 weeks) (p660). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).
new: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Suvorexant and lemborexant are dual orexin receptor antagonists for insomnia. The suvorexant trial in mild–moderate probable Alzheimer dementia randomized 285, of whom 277 completed. Placebo-adjusted total sleep time improved by 28 minutes at week 4 (p660; Herring et al., FDA Belsomra prescribing information). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).

old: General turning interval q2–3h (p683); RCT of 942 NH residents randomized to q2h/q3h/q4h turning (p683) found no significant difference in PI incidence: 2.5% vs 0.6% vs 3.1% (p684).
new: General turning interval q2–3h (p683); RCT of 942 NH residents on high-density foam mattresses randomized to q2h/q3h/q4h turning (p683) found no significant difference in PI incidence: 2.5% vs 0.6% vs 3.1% (p684).

old: Thermography: cooler blanchable erythema predicts necrotic ulcer within 7 days; capacitance devices read in 3–8 seconds (p686).
new: Thermography: in one NH study, areas of blanchable erythema with cooler skin temperatures were more likely to develop necrotic ulcers within 7 days; capacitance devices read in 3–8 seconds (p686).

old: Parenteral empiric: cefazolin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin; vancomycin for MRSA; metronidazole/carbapenem/beta-lactamase inhibitor for anaerobes (p697).
new: Parenteral empiric: cefazolin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin; vancomycin may be required for MRSA; metronidazole/carbapenem/beta-lactamase inhibitor for anaerobes (p697).

old: In the RCT of 942 nursing home residents, did turning every 2, 3, or 4 hours change PI incidence significantly?
new: In the RCT of 942 nursing home residents on high-density foam mattresses, did turning every 2, 3, or 4 hours change PI incidence significantly?

old: No — 2.5% (q2h) vs 0.6% (q3h) vs 3.1% (q4h), not significantly different (p684).
new: No — among residents on high-density foam mattresses, 2.5% (q2h) vs 0.6% (q3h) vs 3.1% (q4h), not significantly different (p684).

old: Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises: 3 sets/day of 15 contractions, building hold from 3 to 10 seconds (p709).
new: Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises: for example, 3 sets/day of 15 contractions, building hold from 3 to 10 seconds (p709).

old: Botulinum toxin A (cystoscopic): effect lasts about 6 months (p715).
new: Botulinum toxin A (cystoscopic): early trial results suggest the effect lasts about 6 months (p715).

old: 30%–50% of institutionalized patients with frequent UI also have fecal incontinence — shared pathophysiology (p716).
new: 30%–50% of institutionalized patients with frequent UI also have fecal incontinence — this coexistence suggests common pathophysiologic mechanisms (p716).

old: What is the recommended pelvic floor (Kegel) exercise regimen?
new: What is an example of a pelvic floor (Kegel) exercise regimen?

old: Three sets daily of 15 contractions, building hold time from 3 to 10 seconds (p709).
new: For example, three sets daily of 15 contractions, building hold time from 3 to 10 seconds (p709).

old: Assess rehab potential only after acute illness resolves — delirium, hemodynamic instability, occult fracture, acute infection delay it (p821).
new: Assess rehab potential after acute illness resolves — delirium, hemodynamic instability, occult fracture, acute infection may delay referral to rehabilitation (p821).

old: Flexibility: 90 degrees knee flexion for stairs; 120 to 150 degrees shoulder flexion/abduction to reach overhead (p825).
new: Flexibility: at least 90 degrees knee flexion for stairs; 120 to 150 degrees shoulder flexion/abduction to reach overhead (p825).

old: Cardiac rehab: only one-third of eligible patients participate (12% in a 600k-patient Medicare cohort) (p830). CR vs. none: mortality 2.3% vs. 5.3%; benefit sustained at 5 years, 16% vs. 25% (p830). ≥25 sessions → 20% lower 5-yr mortality vs. fewer sessions (p830). Heart failure: stable 3 to 4 weeks before starting; CR → 28% lower mortality/hospitalization, 29% lower death rate, peak VO2 +15% to 30%, symptoms/ADLs/well-being +15% to 50%; QoL gains seen as early as 2 months (p830).
new: Cardiac rehab: only one-third of eligible patients participate (12% in a cohort of more than 600,000 Medicare patients) (p830). CR vs. none: mortality 2.3% vs. 5.3%; benefit sustained at 5 years, 16% vs. 25% (p830). ≥25 sessions → 20% lower 5-yr mortality vs. fewer sessions (p830). Heart failure: stable at least 3 to 4 weeks before starting; CR → 28% lower mortality/hospitalization, 29% lower death rate, peak VO2 +15% to 30%, symptoms/ADLs/well-being +15% to 50%; QoL gains seen as early as 2 months (p830).

old: Stroke: rehab can begin as early as 24 to 48 hours poststroke once the patient is medically stable (p831). Dysphagia silent in up to one-third; aphasia in one-third (p831). Bladder incontinence 50% to 70% month 1, back to general-population levels by 6 months (p831). Shoulder pain 34% to 84%; depression 15% to 70% (p831).
new: Stroke: rehab can begin as early as 24 to 48 hours poststroke once the patient is medically stable (p831). Dysphagia can be silent in up to one-third of patients with dysphagia; aphasia in one-third (p831). Bladder incontinence 50% to 70% month 1, back to general-population levels by 6 months (p831). Shoulder pain 34% to 84%; depression 15% to 70% (p831).

old: Post-THA (posterolateral): avoid >90 degrees hip flexion early (p832).
new: Post-THA (posterolateral): may need to avoid more than 90 degrees hip flexion early (p832).

old: End of life: delirium in >80% of patients; for refractory agitated delirium, lorazepam 0.5–1.0 mg PO/IV/SQ is the sedation agent of choice (p890).
new: End of life: delirium in >80% of patients; if sedation is indicated for severe agitated delirium, lorazepam, starting dose 0.5–1.0 mg PO/IV/SQ is the sedation agent of choice (p890).

old: What agent and dose are recommended for sedation in refractory agitated delirium at the end of life?
new: What agent and starting dose are recommended for sedation in severe agitated delirium at the end of life?

old: Citalopram — initial 5–10 mg, max 20 mg/day; CitAD trial showed benefit for agitation, but QTc prolongation and worsened cognition limit its use (p929).
new: Citalopram — initial 5–10 mg, max 20 mg/day; CitAD trial showed benefit for agitation, but QTc prolongation and worsened cognition may limit its use (p929).

old: Melatonin doses up to 10 mg showed little or no sleep benefit in a Cochrane review (p931); one small trial of melatonin 3 mg helped agitation/sundowning (p932); ramelteon showed no sleep benefit (p932).
new: A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence that melatonin doses up to 10 mg may have little or no sleep benefit (p931); one small trial of melatonin 3 mg helped agitation/sundowning (p932); ramelteon showed no sleep benefit (p932).

old: Atypical parkinsonisms (PSP, MSA, CBS) have a combined prevalence of 5% to 10% of PD's (p938).
new: Atypical parkinsonisms (PSP, MSA, CBS) have a prevalence of roughly 5% to 10% of PD's (p938).

old: Amantadine — 100 mg BID for PD symptoms, 300–400 mg/day for antidyskinetic effect; confusion, hallucinations, livedo reticularis; poorly tolerated in older adults (p944). Only established effective antidyskinetic agent (antiglutamatergic).
new: Amantadine, immediate release. The chapter describes 100 mg twice daily for motor symptoms and higher doses for dyskinesia (p944). In older adults, reduced renal clearance may cause accumulation. Use renal-function-adjusted dosing and monitor confusion, hallucinations, edema and livedo reticularis. The chapter's 300–400 mg/day range is not a routine geriatric starting dose (US prescribing information).

old: McKeith criteria: probable DLB = 2 core features, or 1 core + 1 suggestive feature (p984).Current practice (not the book): probable DLB = ≥2 core features, or 1 core feature + ≥1 indicative biomarker (reduced DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, abnormal MIBG scintigraphy, or PSG-confirmed REM sleep without atonia) — DLB Consortium 4th consensus report (McKeith et al.), 2017.
new: Probable DLB: at least two core clinical features, or one core feature plus an indicative biomarker (DLB Consortium 2017). REM sleep behavior disorder is a core feature. For book questions, p984 discusses RBD as core, while the older Table 63-3 uses the term “suggestive” and places RBD in that category.Current practice (not the book): probable DLB = ≥2 core features, or 1 core feature + ≥1 indicative biomarker (reduced DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, abnormal MIBG scintigraphy, or PSG-confirmed REM sleep without atonia) — DLB Consortium 4th consensus report (McKeith et al.), 2017.

old: Mean survival ~10y, disability progressing ~10%/yr (p983).
new: In postmortem-confirmed DLB cases, mean survival ~10y, disability progressing ~10%/yr (p983).

old: Predictors: older age at motor onset, bradykinesia/non-tremor phenotype, bilateral onset, declining levodopa response, depression, hallucinations (p985).
new: Possible predictors: older age at motor onset, bradykinesia/non-tremor phenotype, bilateral onset, declining levodopa response, depression, hallucinations (p985).

old: Orthostatic dx criterion: ≥30 mmHg systolic BP drop (practically, ≥20 systolic/≥10 diastolic considered significant in the absence of an appropriate heart-rate increase) (p986).
new: In the 2022 MDS criteria, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a systolic fall ≥20 mm Hg, usually accompanied by a diastolic fall ≥10 mm Hg, with a blunted heart-rate response. The time window is 3 minutes for clinically established MSA and up to 10 minutes for clinically probable MSA. The 30-mm Hg systolic threshold on p986 reflects earlier criteria.

old: bvFTD accounts for >50% of FTD cases; pathology ~50% tau, ~50% TDP-43, <10% FUS (p987).
new: In most centers, bvFTD accounts for >50% of FTD cases; pathology ~50% tau, ~50% TDP-43, <10% FUS (p987).

old: PPA = isolated language deficit ≥2 years before other decline (p987). nfvPPA: apraxic/agrammatic speech, preserved single-word comprehension; left-dominant atrophy (inferior frontal/insula/caudate); ~20% TDP-43 (type A) at autopsy, remainder tau (CBD > PSP > Pick) (p988). svPPA: fluent but semantically empty speech, surface dyslexia; begins in amygdala/anterior temporal lobe; most behaviorally prominent PPA; usually TDP-43 type C, tau-negative (p988). Logopenic PPA = usually an AD language presentation; may respond to cholinesterase inhibitors (p987).
new: Primary progressive aphasia: insidious, progressive language impairment is the dominant early deficit and the main initial limitation on daily activities. The book describes an older two-year isolated-language criterion (p987). The international consensus criteria do not require waiting two years to diagnose PPA. nfvPPA: apraxic/agrammatic speech, preserved single-word comprehension; left-dominant atrophy (inferior frontal/insula/caudate); ~20% TDP pathology (usually TDP-43 type A) at autopsy, most show tau (CBD > PSP > Pick) (p988). svPPA: fluent but semantically empty speech, surface dyslexia; begins in amygdala/anterior temporal lobe; most behaviorally prominent PPA; often TDP-43 type C-positive, tau-negative inclusions at autopsy (p988). Logopenic PPA = usually an AD language presentation; may respond to cholinesterase inhibitors if imaging or other biomarkers confirm AD etiology (p987-988).

old: Treatment: symptomatic only — SSRIs for behavioral symptoms/cravings/compulsions; atypical neuroleptics only if delusions are problematic; no role for cholinesterase inhibitors (may worsen agitation) (p991).
new: Treatment: symptomatic only — SSRIs for behavioral symptoms/cravings/compulsions; atypical neuroleptics can be considered if delusions are problematic; no theoretical basis for cholinesterase inhibitors (may worsen agitation) (p991).

old: Incidence 1–2/100,000/yr; ~5,000 new US cases/yr; ~2:1 M:F (p991).
new: Incidence 1–2/100,000/yr; ~5,000 new cases/yr; ~2:1 M:F (p991).

old: Symptomatic treatment only; levodopa helps a minority; no role for cholinesterase inhibitors (p992).
new: Symptomatic treatment only; levodopa helps a minority; no theoretical basis for cholinesterase inhibitors (p992).

old: Falls as the first symptom in 60%; downward vertical gaze palsy is more specific than upward (mild vertical gaze limitation is normal with aging), with preserved oculocephalic reflex (p992).
new: Falls as the first symptom in 60%; downward vertical gaze palsy is more specific than upward (mild vertical gaze limitation is normal with aging), with oculocephalic reflex preserved early in disease (p992).

old: Cholinesterase inhibitors — first-line for DLB (often better response than AD, esp. hallucinations); no role in bvFTD/CBD, may worsen agitation (p984, p991–992).
new: Patients with DLB should be offered a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (often better response than AD, esp. hallucinations); no theoretical basis for use in bvFTD/CBD, may worsen agitation (p984, p991–992).

old: Levodopa — helps parkinsonism in DLB (only after hallucinations/fluctuation are controlled), ~1/3 of MSA patients, and some PSP/CBD patients, but efficacy is limited/wanes (p984, p986, p992).
new: Levodopa — can be used if indicated for parkinsonism in DLB (once hallucinations/fluctuation are controlled), ~1/3 of MSA patients, and some PSP/CBD patients, but efficacy is limited/wanes (p984, p986, p992).

old: המשמעות הקלינית: האוטונומיה של חולה כשיר גוברת — אך לפני שמכבדים סירוב, יש חובה לנסות לשכנע אותו לקבל לפחות חמצן, מזון ונוזלים, טיפולים שגרתיים למחלות בו-זמניות/רקע, וטיפול מקל (פליאטיבי).
new: המשמעות הקלינית: יש לכבד את רצונו של חולה הנוטה למות בעל כשרות שאינו רוצה שחייו יוארכו ולהימנע מטיפול בו (§15(א)).

old: אם לאחר מאמץ סביר הוא עדיין מסרב — מכבדים את הסירוב, כולל למזון ונוזלים.
new: בנפרד, על המטפלים לעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנעו לקבל חמצן, מזון ונוזלים אף באמצעים מלאכותיים, טיפולים שגרתיים למחלות בו-זמניות או למחלות רקע וטיפול מקל (§15(ב)).

old: הערה (פרשנות, לא לשון החוק): אין ניגוד בין הוראות אלה; זהו מדרג מכוון: כשיר (15) — סירובו מכובד, גם למזון/נוזלים, לאחר מאמץ סביר לשכנע; לא כשיר, לא בשלב סופי (16) — טיפול נלווה (כולל מזון ונוזלים) מוגן תמיד; לא כשיר, בשלב סופי (17) — נמנעים גם מטיפול נלווה, אך נוזלים מוגנים אלא אם גורמים סבל/נזק.
new: הערה (פרשנות, לא לשון החוק): אין ניגוד בין הוראות אלה; זהו מדרג מכוון: כשיר (15) — סירובו מכובד, גם למזון/נוזלים, ולצד זאת מוטלת חובה נפרדת לעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע; לא כשיר, לא בשלב סופי (16) — טיפול נלווה (כולל מזון ונוזלים) מוגן תמיד; לא כשיר, בשלב סופי (17) — נמנעים גם מטיפול נלווה, אך נוזלים מוגנים אלא אם גורמים סבל/נזק.

old: אם נמנע מהמטופל לחתום — הסכמה בפני שני עדים (§14(ג)); במצב חירום רפואי — בעל פה, ותיעוד בכתב סמוך ככל האפשר (§14(ד)).
new: אם נמנע מהמטופל לחתום — הסכמה בפני שני עדים, ובלבד שדבר ההסכמה והעדות יתועדו בכתב סמוך ככל האפשר לאחר מכן (§14(ג)); במצב חירום רפואי — בעל פה, ותיעוד בכתב סמוך ככל האפשר (§14(ד)).

old: (נוהל 3.4.2 עוסק במטופלים שכבר ב"קוד" משרד הבריאות; לקבלה חדשה לאשפוז מסובסד, ה"סיווג" כסיעודי או תשוש נפש נעשה ע"י הגריאטר המחוזי באמצעות ועדה לפי נוהל 01-09 שבחוזר מינהל רפואה 20/2009, סעיף 3.3 — אותה שרשרת; נוהל 01-09 אינו עוסק בסיעודי-מורכב או בשיקום.)
new: (נוהל 3.4.2 מסדיר קבלה של מטופל חדש שלא היה במימון "קוד" קודם לכן (§3.2), וכן שינוי סטטוס למימון משרד הבריאות המחייב קבלה מלאה וטופס הפניה רשמי גם בהעברה בתוך המוסד (§5.2); לקבלה חדשה לאשפוז מסובסד, ה"סיווג" כסיעודי או תשוש נפש נעשה ע"י הגריאטר המחוזי באמצעות ועדה לפי נוהל 01-09 שבחוזר מינהל רפואה 20/2009, סעיף 3.3 — אותה שרשרת; נוהל 01-09 אינו עוסק בסיעודי-מורכב או בשיקום.)

old: לעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע אותו לקבל מזון ונוזלים (אף באמצעים מלאכותיים), חמצן, טיפולים שגרתיים למחלות בו-זמניות/רקע וטיפול מקל — ורק אז, אם הוא עדיין מסרב, לכבד את סירובו (§15).

old: Medications: withdrawing centrally-acting drugs did NOT significantly reduce falls in the most recent systematic review (5 trials, 1309 participants; RaR 0.98, 95% CI 0.63–1.51) — better to prevent uptake than deprescribe later (p639). Avoid prescribing benzodiazepines/z-drugs/other psychotropics for insomnia unless there is a clear pattern of addiction or inability to complete a withdrawal program; consider nonpharmacological approaches (p639). Vitamin D: no benefit in community-dwelling older adults (even if deficient); may reduce falls in RACF residents (p639).
new: Medications: withdrawing centrally-acting drugs did NOT significantly reduce falls in the most recent systematic review (5 trials, 1309 participants; RaR 0.98, 95% CI 0.63–1.51) — better to prevent uptake than deprescribe later (p639). Avoid prescribing benzodiazepines/z-drugs/other psychotropics for insomnia unless there is a clear pattern of addiction or inability to complete a withdrawal program; consider nonpharmacological approaches (p639). Vitamin D: no benefit in community-dwelling older adults (even if deficient); may reduce falls in RACF residents (p639); Required reading: see AGS Beers 2023 required-article card for anticholinergics with prior falls or fractures (Table 3, p2066)

old: Drugs (Table 44-2, p653): Ropinirole 0.25–4 mg, Pramipexole 0.125–2 mg — caution: augmentation, behavioral disinhibition. Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg — reserve for infrequent dosing (highest augmentation risk). Gabapentin enacarbil 600–1200 mg (only α2δ ligand FDA-approved for RLS), gabapentin 100–1800 mg, pregabalin 300 mg — caution: sedation, suicidal ideation. Clonazepam 0.25–2 mg, temazepam 15–30 mg — limited evidence, cognitive risk. Opiate agents (all off-label) for refractory RLS: codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg, methadone 5–10 mg.Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026.
new: RLS drug selection. The AASM favors gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil and pregabalin when appropriate. FDA-labeled gabapentin enacarbil is 600 mg daily for RLS with normal renal function; 1,200 mg adds adverse effects without additional benefit. Dopamine agonists can cause augmentation and behavioral disinhibition. If pramipexole is chosen, the labeled RLS titration is 0.125–0.5 mg once daily. The labeled ropinirole range begins at 0.25 mg, up to 4 mg daily. Table 44-2 lists carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg for infrequent use because of augmentation. Table 44-2 lists off-label gabapentin 100–1,800 mg and pregabalin 300 mg as studied doses. Adjust for renal function and monitor sedation. The table lists clonazepam 0.25–2 mg and temazepam 15–30 mg, with limited evidence and cognitive/fall risks. Its off-label opioid examples are codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg and methadone 5–10 mg. These are historical table ranges. Specialist assessment of respiratory, dependence and medication risks is essential in refractory RLS (p653; FDA prescribing information for Horizant and pramipexole, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026; Current practice (not the book): AASM conditionally suggests against standard pramipexole, transdermal rotigotine or ropinirole use in adults with RLS because of augmentation with longer-term treatment; evidence certainty is moderate for pramipexole/ropinirole and low for rotigotine; patients prioritizing short-term symptom relief over long-term adverse effects may still choose these agents - AASM 2025, recommendations 12-14, p144

old: Oxybutynin (antimuscarinic) 2.5–5 mg tid — dry mouth, blurry vision, ↑ intraocular pressure, delirium, constipation (p712); patients with dementia must be followed for drug-induced delirium (p713).
new: Oxybutynin (antimuscarinic) 2.5–5 mg tid — dry mouth, blurry vision, ↑ intraocular pressure, delirium, constipation (p712); patients with dementia must be followed for drug-induced delirium (p713); Current practice (not the book): offer an antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist for OAB (Strong recommendation, Grade A); counsel on side effects and potential dementia/cognitive risk with antimuscarinics (Clinical Principles), using shared decision-making and patient preferences; when pharmacotherapy is indicated, consider a beta-3 agonist trial first, as typically preferred in the guideline discussion - AUA/SUFU 2024, statements 16-18 and discussion, p24-27

old: Vaginal estrogen ring — 1 ring every 3 months, for atrophic-vaginitis-related urgency UI; contraindicated with gynecologic cancer history, relative contraindication with breast cancer history (Table 47-12, p712).
new: Vaginal estrogen ring — 1 ring every 3 months, for atrophic-vaginitis-related urgency UI; Table 47-12 (p712) lists a history of gynecologic cancer as a contraindication and breast cancer as a relative contraindication. In practice, cancer type and treatment matter. After inadequate relief with nonhormonal treatment, selected breast-cancer survivors may choose low-dose vaginal estrogen after a risk–benefit discussion. For patients taking an aromatase inhibitor, involve the oncologist in that decision. ACOG clinical consensus, 2021. See AGS Beers 2023 required-article card for systemic versus low-dose vaginal estrogen and the breast-cancer discussion qualification (Table 2, p2061)

old: Screening tools (Table 58-3, p884): 4AT scores 0–12, ≥4 suggests delirium; Nu-DESC scores 0–10.
new: Screening tools (Table 58-3, p884): 4AT scores 0–12, ≥4 suggests delirium; Nu-DESC scores 0–10; Current practice (not the book): when delirium indicators are present, a competent practitioner should assess with 4AT; use CAM-ICU or ICDSC in critical care or the recovery room after surgery; a healthcare professional with relevant expertise makes the final diagnosis if assessment indicates delirium - NICE CG103, recommendations updated 2023, 1.6.1-1.6.2, p11

old: Beers-listed culprits (Table 58-2, p883): anticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids, H2-blockers, meperidine, Z-drugs (zolpidem/eszopiclone/zaleplon), TCAs. Psychoactive drugs should be discontinued or minimized whenever possible (p885).
new: Beers-listed culprits (Table 58-2, p883): anticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids, H2-blockers, meperidine, Z-drugs (zolpidem/eszopiclone/zaleplon), TCAs. Psychoactive drugs should be discontinued or minimized whenever possible (p885); Required reading: see AGS Beers 2023 required-article card for opioids and delirium, including the balanced pain-management caveat (Table 3, p2066)

old: Pimavanserin 34 mg/day — FDA-approved for Parkinson disease psychosis; confusion, edema, hypotension (p928).
new: Pimavanserin 34 mg/day — FDA-approved for Parkinson disease psychosis; confusion, edema, hypotension (p928); Current practice (not the book): brexpiprazole received FDA approval in May 2023 for agitation associated with Alzheimer dementia; its boxed warning states increased mortality in older patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics - AGS Alternatives 2025, Table 3 footnote e, p12; FDA announcement, 11 May 2023, approval and boxed-warning paragraphs

old: DBS (STN or GPi target) — FDA-approved 2002; for motor fluctuations/dyskinesias or medication-refractory tremor; does not improve postural instability or other axial features (p949).
new: DBS (STN or GPi target) — FDA-approved 2002; for motor fluctuations/dyskinesias or medication-refractory tremor; does not improve postural instability or other axial features (p949); Current practice (not the book): NICE recommends subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion as an option for adults with advanced levodopa-responsive Parkinson disease, severe motor fluctuations and hyperkinesia or dyskinesia despite available medicines, only when apomorphine or DBS cannot be used or no longer controls symptoms and the commercial arrangement applies; FDA approved it on 16 October 2024 for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson disease - NICE TA934 2023, 1.1 p4; FDA NDA216962 approval package cover and approval letter p1

old: 3 tiers by comorbidity/function/cognition: Good, Intermediate, Poor health.
new: 3 tiers by comorbidity/function/cognition: Good, Intermediate, Poor health; Current practice (not the book): individualize targets (grade C): healthy older adults with few stable illnesses and intact cognition/function should have lower goals such as A1C <7.0-7.5% and/or CGM time in 70-180 mg/dL ≥70% and time ≤70 mg/dL ≤4%; complex/intermediate health prioritizes hypoglycemia avoidance, with less stringent goals such as A1C <8.0%, time in 70-180 mg/dL ≥50% and time <70 mg/dL <1%, considering cognition/function, frailty, comorbidity, medication risk-benefit and preferences; very complex/poor health avoids reliance on A1C and focuses on avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia, with no numerical CGM goal specified; fasting/premeal and bedtime ranges respectively are 80-130/80-180 mg/dL (healthy), 90-150/100-180 (complex/intermediate) and 100-180/110-200 (very complex/poor); lower A1C goals require no recurrent/severe hypoglycemia or undue treatment burden - ADA Standards of Care 2026, Section 13, recommendations 13.7a-c pS282 and Table 13.2 pS284

old: Sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide 2.5–10 mg qd–BID) (p1577). Cautions: hypoglycemia; avoid glyburide — long half-life, not recommended in older adults (p1579); avoid in renal/hepatic impairment (p1579).
new: Sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide 2.5–10 mg qd–BID) (p1577). Cautions: hypoglycemia; avoid glyburide — long half-life, not recommended in older adults (p1579); avoid in renal/hepatic impairment (p1579); Required reading: see AGS Beers 2023 required-article card for qualified sulfonylurea avoidance and the preference if one is used (Table 2, p2061)

old: Vision: first-eye cataract surgery → 34% fewer falls; second-eye surgery similar (~32%) but not statistically significant; one prospective cohort study associated cataract surgery with fewer falls provided post-op spectacle lens power updates were cautious (less than ±0.75 diopter change) (p639). Updating glasses to correct prescription: evidence less clear — one RCT found no significant reduction, and another (vision assessment + treatment) increased falls by ~50% (p639). Single-lens distance glasses for habitual multifocal wearers: 40% fewer falls in the outdoor-active subgroup (p639). Home-safety modification for severe uncorrectable low vision: 41% fewer falls (p639).
new: Vision: first-eye cataract surgery → 34% fewer falls; second-eye surgery similar (~32%) but not statistically significant; one prospective cohort study associated cataract surgery with fewer falls provided post-op spectacle lens power updates were cautious (less than ±0.75 diopter change) (p639). Updating glasses to correct prescription: evidence less clear — one RCT found no significant reduction, and another (vision assessment + treatment) increased falls by ~50% (p639). Single-lens distance glasses plus counseling about ground-level hazards for habitual multifocal wearers: 40% fewer falls in the outdoor-active subgroup (p639). Home-safety modification for severe uncorrectable low vision: 41% fewer falls (p639).

old: Movement is the key screen: none developed PI with >50 spontaneous body movements/night vs 90% PI with ≤20 movements/night (p682).
new: In one monitored geriatric study, none developed PI with >50 spontaneous body movements/night vs 90% PI with ≤20 movements/night (p682).

old: Ultrasound detects damage before clinical signs: ~80% with abnormal images had no documented erythema (p686).
new: Early work suggests ultrasound may detect damage before clinical signs: ~80% with abnormal images had no documented erythema (p686).

old: PVR interpretation: PVR < 100 mL normal; PVR > 200 mL abnormal; 100–200 mL is equivocal (p707).
new: PVR interpretation: PVR < 100 mL without straining generally reflects adequate emptying; PVR > 200 mL abnormal; 100–200 mL is equivocal (p707).

old: Diabetic foot disease: Medicare covers one pair of shoes/inserts each year (p829).
new: Diabetes and severe diabetic foot disease: Medicare covers one pair of therapeutic shoes and inserts or shoe modifications each year (p829).

old: NIA-AA dementia criteria (Table 59-1): decline from previous level that interferes with function, not explained by delirium or major psychiatric disorder; history from patient and a knowledgeable informant + objective cognitive assessment (p895).
new: NIA-AA dementia criteria (Table 59-1): decline from previous level that interferes with function, not explained by delirium or major psychiatric disorder; history from patient and a knowledgeable informant + objective cognitive assessment; impairment involves at least two cognitive or behavioral domains (p895).

old: AChEIs (mainstay): donepezil (Aricept), galantamine (Razadyne), rivastigmine (Exelon) — the text says start low with dose increases approximately every 2 months (p911), while Table 59-7 lists drug-specific steps: donepezil 4–6 wk before 5→10 mg (the 10→23 mg step after 3 months on 10 mg) (p912), galantamine ≥4 wk per step (p912), rivastigmine ≥2 wk per oral step or 4–6 wk for the patch (p913); 18–48% show cognitive improvement, most others just have slowed decline (p911). Cautions: GI upset (take with food); bradycardia/AV block/syncope/weight loss are triggers to deprescribe.
new: AChEIs (mainstay): donepezil (Aricept), galantamine (Razadyne), rivastigmine (Exelon) — the text says start low with dose increases approximately every 2 months (p911), while Table 59-7 lists drug-specific steps: donepezil 4–6 wk before 5→10 mg (the 10→23 mg step after 3 months on 10 mg) (p912), galantamine ≥4 wk per step (p912), rivastigmine ≥2 wk per oral step or 4–6 wk for the patch (p912); 18–48% show cognitive improvement, most others just have slowed decline (p911). Cautions: GI upset (take with food); bradycardia/AV block/syncope/weight loss are triggers to deprescribe.

old: Memantine (Namenda) — NMDA-receptor antagonist, approved for moderate-to-severe AD; combo with an AChEI is not superior to either drug alone (p911).
new: Memantine (Namenda) — NMDA-receptor antagonist, approved for moderate-to-severe AD; combo with an AChEI has not been shown to be superior to either drug alone (p911).

old: Feeding tubes are not recommended in advanced AD — they do not prolong survival or improve comfort, and do not reduce pressure sores, infection, or aspiration risk (p916).
new: Feeding tubes are not recommended in advanced AD — they do not prolong survival or improve comfort, and have not been shown to reduce pressure sores, infection, or aspiration risk (p916).

old: New-onset acute NPS work-up: CBC, chem panel, LFTs, UA/culture; consider TSH, B12, folate, tox screen, ECG; chest x-ray if respiratory signs; imaging particularly if focal signs; EEG if seizure suspected; CSF rarely needed — only if meningitis/encephalitis suspected (p922).
new: New-onset acute NPS work-up: CBC, chem panel, LFTs, UA/culture; consider TSH, B12, folate, tox screen, ECG; chest x-ray if respiratory signs; imaging particularly if focal signs; EEG if seizure suspected; CSF rarely needed — indicated if meningitis/encephalitis suspected (p922). Interpret urine findings in context. With delirium and bacteriuria alone, and no urinary symptoms, fever or hemodynamic instability, assess other causes and observe rather than treating bacteriuria. IDSA, recommendation V.1.

old: Delirium-related agitation (short-term, low-dose), all q6h PRN: haloperidol 0.25–0.5 mg PO/IV, quetiapine 12.5–25 mg PO, olanzapine 2.5 mg PO or 1.25–2.5 mg IM, or risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg PO/IV (p923).Current practice (not the book): risperidone is not given IV; the only injectable form (Risperdal Consta) is IM only — "Do not administer intravenously" — Risperdal Consta prescribing information (Janssen).
new: For significant delirium-related agitation requiring short-term medication, the chapter gives these low PRN doses at six-hour intervals (p923). Haloperidol 0.25–0.5 mg orally (IV only with appropriate monitoring), quetiapine 12.5–25 mg orally, olanzapine 2.5 mg orally or 1.25–2.5 mg IM, or risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg orally. There is no approved IV risperidone formulation.Current practice (not the book): risperidone is not given IV; Risperdal Consta is IM only — "Do not administer intravenously" — Risperdal Consta prescribing information (Janssen).

old: Peak-dose dyskinesia: reduce levodopa dose, or add amantadine (start 100 mg BID, up to 200 mg BID); buspirone up to 20 mg/day (p946).
new: For peak-dose dyskinesia, consider smaller levodopa doses or amantadine when appropriate. The chapter describes 100–200 mg twice daily in selected patients (p946). For immediate-release amantadine, tailor initiation and escalation to renal function, age and neuropsychiatric tolerability. The text also describes buspirone up to 20 mg/day in selected patients.

old: Possible bvFTD needs 3 of 6 core symptoms (early disinhibition, apathy, loss of sympathy/empathy, repetitive motor behaviors, hyperorality, executive deficit) (p982).
new: Possible bvFTD needs 3 of 6 core symptoms (early disinhibition, apathy, loss of sympathy/empathy, repetitive motor behaviors, hyperorality, frontal executive deficit with relative visuospatial sparing) (p982).

old: Osteoarthritis (OA): 60% of adults ≥65 yr have arthritis/chronic joint pain (p1066); intra-articular steroid (40–80 mg depot preparation, verified against the page image) is more effective than placebo in the short term (<3 months), long-term benefit not well established; hyaluronic acid typically 1–5 injections; platelet-rich plasma (PRP) shows efficacy up to 12 months in some studies (p1067)
new: Osteoarthritis (OA): 60% of adults ≥65 yr have arthritis/chronic joint pain (p1066); for knee OA, intra-articular steroid (40–80 mg depot preparation) is more effective than placebo in the short term (<3 months), long-term benefit not well established; hyaluronic acid typically 1–5 injections; platelet-rich plasma (PRP) shows promising efficacy in knee OA up to 12 months in some studies; hip HA/PRP efficacy needs further study (p1067)

old: Table 75-6 tiers — indications (actual replacement criteria): symptomatic + severe AI regardless of LV function, OR asymptomatic + severe AI + EF < 50%, OR severe AI undergoing other cardiac surgery; considerations: asymptomatic, normal LV function, dilated ventricle with LVESD > 50 mm, or moderate AI undergoing other cardiac surgery; possible indication: asymptomatic, normal function, progressive LV dilatation > 65 mm if surgical risk is low (table does not name the dimension; the text calls it LVESD) (p1155).Current practice (not the book): the 65-mm AR threshold is LV end-diastolic dimension (LVEDD >65 mm, progressive, low surgical risk: may be considered); LVESD >50 mm is the end-systolic trigger — ACC/AHA valvular guideline, 2020.
new: Severe chronic AR: symptoms are an indication for surgery regardless of EF when intervention is appropriate. In asymptomatic patients, the 2020 ACC/AHA threshold for LV systolic dysfunction is LVEF ≤55% without another cause. LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m², and progressive LVEDD >65 mm in selected low-risk patients, represent distinct pathways. Severe AR at other cardiac surgery is an additional indication. Table 75-6 prints an older EF threshold of <50% and lists moderate AR during other cardiac surgery as a consideration (p1155).Current practice (not the book): the 65-mm AR threshold is LV end-diastolic dimension (LVEDD >65 mm, progressive, low surgical risk: may be considered); LVESD >50 mm is the end-systolic trigger — ACC/AHA valvular guideline, 2020.

old: Repair durability: reoperation rate ~7–10% at 10 yr, said to equal replacement's own reoperation rate (p1159).
new: Mitral repair durability: p1159 describes good durability but prints 7–10% as “freedom from reoperation,” an inconsistent endpoint label. In a surgical cohort of 1,604 patients, actual freedom from reoperation after repair was 93.6% at 10 years. Durability depends on anatomy, repair technique and population.

old: Spironolactone — 12.5–50 mg daily; eplerenone — 25–50 mg daily; both contraindicated if creatinine ≥2.5 mg/dL or hyperkalemia (p1181).Current practice (not the book): eGFR ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m² or serum potassium ≥5.0 mEq/L are contraindications to MRA initiation — AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022.
new: Steroidal MRAs for symptomatic HFrEF: initiate if eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m² and serum K <5.0 mEq/L, then monitor both. The chapter lists spironolactone 12.5–50 mg daily and eplerenone 25–50 mg daily and gives an older creatinine cutoff (p1181). DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced demonstrated improvements in their HF/CV composite outcomes, including in patients without diabetes. Mortality effects differed between trials.Current practice (not the book): eGFR ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m² or serum potassium ≥5.0 mEq/L are contraindications to MRA initiation — AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022.

old: Azithromycin 250 mg daily or 3×/week reduces exacerbations in former smokers; watch for QTc, hearing loss, resistance (p1254).
new: Azithromycin 250 mg daily or 3×/week reduces exacerbations in former smokers; watch for QTc, hearing loss, resistance; maintenance may be considered for frequent exacerbators despite maximal triple inhalers when worsening airflow obstruction and airway inflammation drive symptoms, without hearing impairment, resting tachycardia or other arrhythmia, apparent QTc-prolongation risk, or clinical/radiographic NTM evidence, with NTM assessment before regular use (p1254).

old: Renal vein renin ratio ≥1.5 between kidneys predicts a beneficial BP response to revascularization; failure to lateralize does not predict a negative response (p1289).
new: Renal vein renin ratio ≥1.5 between kidneys predicts a beneficial BP response to revascularization; failure to lateralize does not predict a negative response; overall BP response cannot be predicted confidently with renal vein renin measurements (p1289).

old: Rome IV: ≥2 of the following, on >25% of occasions, for ≥12 wk in the last 12 mo: ≤2 BM/week, straining, hard stool (Bristol 1-2), sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal obstruction, manual maneuvers to defecate (p1354).
new: Rome IV functional constipation requires at least two features: straining, hard or lumpy stool (Bristol 1–2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal blockage, manual maneuvers (each in more than 25% of defecations), or fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements/week; criteria must be met during the last 3 months, with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis, rare loose stools without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS (Rome Foundation, C2); Hazzard Table 87-1 prints 12 weeks in the last 12 months (p1354).

old: Normal perineal descent is <4 cm (p1365). Plain x-ray: megacolon = colon diameter >6.5 cm; rectal dilatation >4 cm implies dysmotility (p1365).
new: Normal perineal descent is <4 cm (p1365). Plain x-ray: colon diameter >6.5 cm without acute obstruction points toward megacolon; rectal dilatation >4 cm implies dysmotility (p1365).

old: Senna — 1-3 tabs at bedtime; onset 8-12 h (p1372); cheap, safe first-line stimulant.
new: Senna — 1-3 tabs at bedtime if symptoms persist after bulk laxatives in ambulant older people (Table 87-11, p1378); onset 8-12 h (p1372); cheap, safe first-line stimulant.

old: PEG — more potent hyperosmolar laxative than lactulose; disimpaction regimen 1 L (8 sachets)/day × 3 days achieved 89% success (p1376); caution: liquid stools.
new: PEG — more potent hyperosmolar laxative than lactulose; a trial of PEG plus electrolytes for disimpaction at 1 L (8 sachets)/day × 3 days achieved 89% success (p1376); caution: liquid stools.

old: ≥2 of: ≤2 BM/wk, straining, hard stool (Bristol 1-2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal obstruction sensation, manual maneuvers — on >25% of occasions for ≥12 wk in the last 12 mo (p1354).
new: At least two features: fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements/week, or straining, Bristol 1–2 stools, incomplete evacuation, blockage or manual maneuvers in more than 25% of defecations; symptoms fulfill criteria for the last three months and began at least six months before diagnosis, loose stools are rare without laxatives, and IBS criteria are insufficient (Rome Foundation, C2); Table 87-1 (p1354) gives a different time window.

old: FNA indicated: nodules ≥1 cm solid + hypoechoic; ≥1.5 cm isoechoic/hyperechoic solid; abnormal cervical lymph nodes. FNA or observation: mixed cystic-solid or spongiform nodules ≥2 cm. FNA not required: purely cystic nodules or nodules <1 cm (Table 98-8, p1555).
new: FNA indicated: nodules ≥1 cm solid + hypoechoic; ≥1.5 cm isoechoic/hyperechoic solid; abnormal cervical lymph nodes. FNA or observation: mixed cystic-solid or spongiform nodules ≥2 cm. FNA not required: purely cystic nodules or nodules <1 cm; low TSH prompts radionuclide scanning, and functioning hot nodules do not require cytologic evaluation (Table 98-8, p1555).

old: FNA not required: purely cystic nodules or nodules <1 cm (p1555).
new: FNA not required: purely cystic nodules or nodules <1 cm; low TSH prompts radionuclide scanning, and functioning hot nodules do not require cytologic evaluation (p1555).

old: Metformin / metformin ER: printed dose lines 500–1000 mg BID, max 2500 mg/d, 500–2000 mg qd — the page does not pair each line to an agent (p1577). Cautions: avoid if eGFR <30; avoid in unstable heart failure/acute illness (lactic-acidosis risk) (p1576).
new: Metformin / metformin ER: printed dose lines 500–1000 mg BID, max 2500 mg/d, 500–2000 mg qd — the page does not pair each line to an agent (p1577). Cautions: avoid if eGFR <30; avoid in unstable heart failure or during acute hospitalization for major illness that could reduce tissue perfusion (lactic-acidosis risk) (p1576).

old: PCV13 should be given first, with PPSV given at least 8 weeks later, per ACIP (p1690).Current practice (not the book): PCV15, PCV20 or PCV21 for adults ≥50; after PCV15 give PPSV23 one year later (8 weeks for certain conditions); no PPSV23 after PCV20/PCV21 — CDC, 2026.
new: PCV13 should be given first, with PPSV given at least 8 weeks later, per ACIP (p1690).Current practice (not the book): prior vaccination determines the schedule: PCV15, PCV20 or PCV21 for adults ≥50 who never received a PCV or whose history is unknown; after PCV15 give PPSV23 if not previously administered, one year later (8 weeks for certain conditions); no PPSV23 after PCV20/PCV21 — CDC, 2026.

old: Study summary of Chapter 74 - Coronary Heart Disease and Dyslipidemia; the book and the full chapter are the reference.
new: Study summary of Chapter 74 - Coronary Heart Disease and Dyslipidemia; the book and the full chapter are the reference; additional current-practice valve reading: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 with corrections.

old: Study summary of Chapter 75; the book and the full chapter are the reference.
new: Study summary of Chapter 75; the book and the full chapter are the reference; additional current-practice valve reading: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 with corrections.

old: Table 75-15 (INR targets + aspirin): mechanical aortic valve INR 2–3 (2.5–3.5 with risk factors), mechanical mitral valve INR 2.5–3.5 always; bioprosthetic INR 2–3 for 3 months only if no risk factors — with risk factors, bioprosthetic mitral rises to INR 2.5–3.5 (bioprosthetic aortic stays 2–3, no stated 3-mo limit); aspirin 75–325 mg/day with a mechanical valve, 75–100 mg/day with a bioprosthetic valve (p1161).Current practice (not the book): with a mechanical valve on warfarin, adding aspirin 75–100 mg daily may be considered when bleeding risk is low (Class 2b), not routinely — ACC/AHA valvular guideline, 2020.
new: Prosthetic valves: mechanical valves require VKA therapy, with INR target based on valve, position and thromboembolic risk (typically 2.5 for a current-generation mechanical aortic valve without added risk and 3.0 for mechanical mitral valves). US guidance considers VKA to target INR 2.5 for 3–6 months after selected surgical bioprosthetic aortic or mitral replacement. An independent indication may warrant ongoing anticoagulation. Table 75-15 prints an older routine aspirin combination and different bioprosthetic regimens (p1161).Current practice (not the book): with a mechanical valve on VKA, adding low-dose aspirin 75–100 mg/day for antiplatelet therapy requires a separate indication (ESC/EACTS: concomitant symptomatic atherosclerotic disease) and low bleeding risk; ESC/EACTS 2025 class IIa, level B — ESC/EACTS 2025, Eur Heart J 2025;46:4635; ACC/AHA 2020 class 2b, level B-R — ACC/AHA 2020, Circulation 2021;143:e142.

old: The cited p938 and p941 discuss the syndromes; Chapter 63 links longer exposure to repetitive head impacts with neocortical Lewy body disease and links that pathology with parkinsonism and dementia (p938, p941, p999).
new: Pages 938 and 941 describe the syndromes; Chapter 64 links longer exposure to repetitive head impacts with neocortical Lewy body disease and links that pathology with parkinsonism and dementia (p938, p941, p999).

old: Cardiac rehab: only one-third of eligible patients participate (12% in a 600k-patient Medicare cohort) (p830). CR vs. none: mortality 2.3% vs. 5.3%; benefit sustained at 5 years, 16% vs. 25% (p830). ≥25 sessions → 20% lower 5-yr mortality vs. fewer sessions (p830). Heart failure: stable at least 3 to 4 weeks before starting; CR → 28% lower mortality/hospitalization, 29% lower death rate, peak VO2 +15% to 30%, symptoms/ADLs/well-being +15% to 50%; QoL gains seen as early as 2 months (p830).
new: Cardiac rehab: only one-third of eligible patients participate (12% in a cohort of more than 600,000 Medicare patients) (p830). CR vs. none: mortality 2.3% vs. 5.3%; benefit sustained at 5 years, 16% vs. 25% (p830). ≥25 sessions → 20% lower 5-yr mortality vs. fewer sessions (p830). Heart failure: stable at least 3 to 4 weeks before starting; CR → 28% lower mortality/hospitalization, 29% lower death rate, peak VO2 +15% to 30%, symptoms/ADLs/well-being +15% to 50%; QoL gains seen as early as 2 months (p830).

old: CVD-outcome-proven drug classes (large CVOTs, average participant age >60): SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin) and GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide) (p1571).
new: CVD-outcome-proven drug classes (large CVOTs, average participant age >60): SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin) and GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide) (p1570–1571).

old: Women affected 2–3× more than men overall, but this gender parity disappears in old age (p1608) — LORA occurs with roughly equal M:F (p1610)
new: Women affected 2–3× more than men overall, but the female predominance narrows in late-onset disease (p1608) — LORA occurs with roughly equal M:F (p1610)

old: Vectra DA: FDA-approved 12-protein multibiomarker blood test for RA disease activity, complements (does not replace) clinical judgment (p1612)
new: Vectra DA: laboratory-developed 12-protein blood test for RA disease activity, complements (does not replace) clinical judgment (p1612; Labcorp Vectra sample report, test 504965, documents its regulatory status)

old: Glucocorticoid dose-response in Medicare beneficiaries >75 yr: ≤5 mg, >5–10 mg, >10 mg/day → 20%, 32%, 47% increased serious-infection risk vs 13% in non-users (p1618)Current practice (not the book): in the source (Medicare RA patients ≥75 y on stable DMARDs) 12.8/20.0/32.0/46.8 are crude hospitalized-infection rates per 100 person-years, not % increased risk; adjusted HRs vs no glucocorticoid 1.31, 1.74, 2.23 — George et al., Ann Intern Med 2020, Table 3.
new: Glucocorticoid dose-response in Medicare patients aged 75 or older: ≤5 mg, >5–10 mg, >10 mg/day → approximately 20, 32 and 47 hospitalized infections per 100 person-years, respectively, versus 13 per 100 person-years without glucocorticoids (p1618)Current practice (not the book): in the source (Medicare RA patients ≥75 y on stable DMARDs) 12.8/20.0/32.0/46.8 are crude hospitalized-infection rates per 100 person-years, not % increased risk; adjusted HRs vs no glucocorticoid 1.31, 1.74, 2.23 — George et al., Ann Intern Med 2020, Table 3.

old: Belimumab (anti-BAFF) — first lupus drug in its class to get FDA approval, 2011, indication expanded to lupus nephritis 2021; voclosporin (oral calcineurin inhibitor) also approved for active lupus nephritis, role in older patients untested (p1621–1622)
new: Belimumab (anti-BAFF) — first lupus drug in its class to get FDA approval, 2011, indication expanded to adult active lupus nephritis in December 2020; voclosporin (oral calcineurin inhibitor) also approved for active lupus nephritis, role in older patients untested (p1621–1622; FDA supplemental approval letter, December 2020)

old: mRNA vaccines preferred over J&J; immunosuppressed patients get an extra dose ≥28 days after primary series (p1627–1628)
new: Historical vaccine schedule in this edition: mRNA vaccines were preferred to J&J, and an extra dose at least 28 days after completing the two-dose mRNA primary series was advised for immunosuppressed patients (p1627)

old: Typical RA affects women 2–3× more than men, but this gender parity disappears in old age (p1608) — LORA occurs with roughly equal frequency in men and women (p1610).
new: Typical RA affects women 2–3× more than men, but the female predominance narrows in late-onset disease (p1608) — LORA occurs with roughly equal frequency in men and women (p1610).

old: ≤5 mg, >5–10 mg, and >10 mg/day of glucocorticoid conferred 20%, 32%, and 47% increased risk of serious infection respectively, versus 13% in non-users (p1618).
new: ≤5 mg, >5–10 mg, and >10 mg/day of glucocorticoid were associated with approximately 20, 32 and 47 hospitalized infections per 100 person-years, respectively, versus 13 per 100 person-years without glucocorticoids (p1618; George et al., Table 3).

old: FDA-approved in 2011 as the first lupus drug in its class (anti-BAFF); indication expanded to active lupus nephritis in 2021 (p1621–1622).
new: FDA-approved in 2011 as the first lupus drug in its class (anti-BAFF); indication expanded to adult active lupus nephritis in December 2020 (p1621–1622; FDA supplemental approval letter, December 2020).

old: Evidence for prophylaxis in PJ (prosthetic joint) patients is even weaker than for prosthetic valves; despite this, the ADA recommends "considering" antibiotic prophylaxis for PJs at "high risk" — placed within 2 years, or in immunosuppressed patients (including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, malnourishment), or with prior joint infection (p1674–1675)Current practice (not the book): in general, prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended before dental procedures to prevent prosthetic joint infection — ADA clinical practice guideline, 2015.
new: Evidence for prophylaxis in PJ (prosthetic joint) patients is even weaker than for prosthetic valves; the historical discussion describes considering antibiotic prophylaxis for PJs deemed "high risk" — placed within 2 years, or in immunosuppressed patients (including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, malnourishment), or with prior joint infection (p1674–1675)Current practice (not the book): in general, prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended before dental procedures to prevent prosthetic joint infection — ADA clinical practice guideline, 2015.

old: Treatment is tiered: vancomycin first-line; fidaxomicin equivalent for cure and lowers relapse but costlier (limits first-line use); metronidazole no longer first-line "except in serious disease with vancomycin" (p1672); for C difficile colitis/toxic megacolon, vancomycin + metronidazole IV "if ileus or toxic megacolon" (p1673); vancomycin prophylaxis in patients with recent CDI needing further antibiotics reduces risk to 4% from 26% (p1672–1673, Table 104-1)
new: For initial nonfulminant CDI, IDSA/SHEA favors fidaxomicin when feasible; oral vancomycin remains an acceptable alternative; metronidazole is not first-line monotherapy (p1672); for fulminant CDI, combine enteral vancomycin and IV metronidazole, especially with ileus (p1673); a study of patients with recent CDI needing other antibiotics reported recurrence of 4% with oral vancomycin prophylaxis versus 26% without it; this was a historical study result. AGA 2026 advises against giving vancomycin during systemic antibiotics for the purpose of CDI prevention (p1672–1673, Table 104-1; AGA, advice 12)

old: HAP = onset >48 h after admission or within 10-14 days after a hospital discharge (p1681).
new: Hospital-acquired pneumonia begins at least 48 h after admission and was not incubating on arrival; Hazzard also discusses recent discharge (10–14 days) as a healthcare exposure, which alone does not define HAP (p1681).

old: SCAP severity score (Table 105-5, p1686): major criteria — pH <7.30 (13 pts), SBP <90 mm Hg (11 pts); minor criteria — confusion (5 pts), BUN >30 mg/dL (5 pts), RR >30 (9 pts), multilobar/bilateral CXR (5 pts), PaO2 <54 mm Hg or PaO2/FiO2 <250 (6 pts), age ≥80 (5 pts); risk — low 0-1 (<10 pts), intermediate 2 (10-19 pts), high 3-4 (>20 pts).
new: SCAP severity score (Table 105-5, p1686): major criteria — pH <7.30 (13 pts), SBP <90 mm Hg (11 pts); minor criteria — confusion (5 pts), BUN >30 mg/dL (5 pts), RR >30 (9 pts), multilobar/bilateral CXR (5 pts), PaO2 <54 mm Hg or PaO2/FiO2 <250 (6 pts), age ≥80 (5 pts); risk — low 0-1 (<10 pts), intermediate 2 (10-19 pts), high 3-4 (>20 points [sic]; the printed footnote leaves exactly 20 unassigned).

old: SMART-COP score (Table 105-6, p1687): SBP <90 (2 pts), multilobar involvement (1 pt), albumin <3.5 g/dL (1 pt), RR age-adjusted (1 pt: <50y ≥25/min, ≥50y ≥30/min), tachycardia ≥125 (1 pt), confusion (1 pt), oxygenation age-adjusted (2 pts: <50y PaO2 <70 or SpO2 ≤93% or PaO2/FiO2 <333; ≥50y PaO2 <60 or SpO2 ≤90% or PaO2/FiO2 <250), pH <7.35 (2 pts); risk for needing vasopressor/intensive respiratory support — 0-2 low, 3-4 moderate, 5-6 high, ≥7 very high.
new: SMART-COP score (Table 105-6, p1687): SBP <90 (2 pts), multilobar involvement (1 pt), albumin <3.5 g/dL (1 pt), RR age-adjusted (1 pt: <50y ≥25/min, ≥50y ≥30/min), tachycardia ≥125 (1 pt), confusion (1 pt), oxygenation age-adjusted (2 pts: <50y PaO2 <70 or SpO2 ≤93% or PaO2/FiO2 <333; ≥50y PaO2 <60 or SpO2 ≤90% or PaO2/FiO2 <250), pH <7.35 (2 pts); risk for needing vasopressor/intensive respiratory support — 0-2 low, 3-4 moderate, 5-6 high, ≥7 very high [sic, printed age boundary]. Current practice (not the book): The original SMART-COP rule places a patient aged exactly 50 in the younger group. Charles et al., 2008, SMART-COP.

old: Standard latent-TB regimen: isoniazid 9 months; alternative rifampin 4 months; isoniazid + rifapentine 12 weeks also effective (p1694).
new: For latent TB, short rifamycin-based regimens are preferred when suitable, including rifampin 4 months or isoniazid plus rifapentine 12 weeks; isoniazid 9 months is an alternative when rifamycins are unsuitable (p1694; NTCA/CDC latent tuberculosis treatment guideline, 2020).

old: Drug-resistant TB varies with the resistance pattern; in general, multidrug-resistant TB needs 18-24 months with 4-5 active drugs guided by susceptibility (p1694).
new: Drug-resistant TB varies with the resistance pattern; the book describes older 18–24 month regimens, but current guidance recommends six-month regimens for eligible adults with rifampin-resistant pulmonary TB, selected according to susceptibility and treatment history (p1694; ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA guideline update, 2025).

old: HD-IIV4 (high-dose) has 4× the antigen dose of standard-dose vaccine and is more effective in older adults; aIIV4 (MF59-adjuvanted) also shows increased immunogenicity and is linked in observational studies to reduced hospitalization for flu, pneumonia, and cardiovascular events; RIV4 (recombinant) also promising. ACIP endorses any of these for older adults (p1735).
new: The edition’s HD-IIV4 (high-dose) has 4× the antigen dose of standard-dose vaccine and is more effective in older adults; aIIV4 (MF59-adjuvanted) also shows increased immunogenicity and is linked in observational studies to reduced hospitalization for flu, pneumonia, and cardiovascular events; RIV4 (recombinant) also promising. Current US ACIP guidance preferentially recommends age-appropriate high-dose, adjuvanted, or recombinant influenza vaccine for adults 65 or older; the seasonal formulations are now trivalent (p1735).

old: Peramivir (IV) — FDA-approved 2015, IV-only formulation (p1736).
new: Peramivir (IV) — first FDA-approved in December 2014, IV-only formulation (p1736; FDA original approval, application 206426).

old: Asymptomatic/presymptomatic transmission was estimated in one study to account for up to 79% of documented cases (p1738).
new: An early model attributed 79% of documented cases to people whose infections were undocumented; undocumented infection could include mild symptoms (p1738).

old: Vaccine candidates demonstrated >90% effectiveness against infection (p1740).
new: The original randomized mRNA vaccine trials demonstrated over 90% efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19; preventing all infections was a different endpoint (p1740; Polack et al., 2020, and Baden et al., 2021).

old: Unlike SARS-CoV/MERS (which replicate mainly in the lower respiratory tract), SARS-CoV-2 achieves high viral loads in the upper respiratory tract, and shedding peaks at the very start of infection — enabling presymptomatic spread; transmission through asymptomatic or presymptomatic cases was estimated in one study to account for up to 79% of documented cases (p1738).
new: Unlike SARS-CoV/MERS (which replicate mainly in the lower respiratory tract), SARS-CoV-2 achieves high viral loads in the upper respiratory tract, and shedding peaks at the very start of infection — enabling presymptomatic spread; the early modeling estimate of 79% concerned previously undocumented infections, including infections with mild symptoms (p1738).

old: Of the variants discussed, only the APOE finding had replicated in multiple studies.
new: In the genome-wide screens reviewed in this chapter, only the APOE association had appeared in multiple studies.

old: Medication may be appropriate when distress or risk of harm makes the balance favorable.
new: For dementia-related behavior, Beers reserves antipsychotics for a substantial threat of harm to the patient or others when non-drug measures have failed or cannot be used.

old: In Parkinson disease/dementia trials, honey-thick fluids reduced immediate aspiration more than nectar-thick or chin-down strategies, but chin-down and thickened fluids were equally effective for pneumonia prevention over 3 months (p450).
new: In Parkinson disease/dementia trials, honey-thick fluids reduced immediate aspiration more than nectar-thick or chin-down strategies, but the trial found no significant difference in pneumonia incidence between chin-down and thickened fluids over 3 months (p450; Robbins et al., PMID 18378947).

old: Core temperature below 32°C requires active core rewarming. Severe cases require intensive supportive care and ECG monitoring (p584).
new: Below 32°C, start active rewarming and monitor ECG, temperature and circulation. Stable patients can receive active external rewarming with warmed fluids when indicated. Escalate to specialist core or extracorporeal rewarming for failure to rewarm, hemodynamic instability or cardiac arrest (p584; European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2025, Special Circumstances).

old: Influenza. With less antibody production after standard vaccination, increasing the antigen dose or adding an adjuvant can improve the response. In the trial described, high-dose vaccine gave a 24% relative reduction in influenza-like illness compared with standard dose. Antibody titers and clinical illness are different outcomes (p59–60).
new: Influenza. With less antibody production after standard vaccination, increasing the antigen dose or adding an adjuvant can improve the response. In the trial described, high-dose vaccine gave 24% relative efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza with protocol-defined influenza-like illness compared with standard dose. Antibody titers and clinical illness are different outcomes (p59–60; DíazGranados et al., NEJM 2014, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1315727).

old: Influenza high-dose/adjuvanted formulations can improve responses. One trial found 24% relative efficacy for high-dose versus standard-dose vaccine against influenza-like illness (p60).
new: Influenza high-dose/adjuvanted formulations can improve responses. One trial found 24% relative efficacy for high-dose versus standard-dose vaccine against laboratory-confirmed influenza with protocol-defined influenza-like illness (p60; DíazGranados et al., NEJM 2014).

old: Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS): 7-category clinician-judgment scale derived from FI work; similar predictive power to FI for institutionalization/death (p623)
new: Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS): the original seven-category version used clinical judgment and predicted institutionalization and death similarly to the FI (p623). The current CFS has nine levels.

old: Table 42-3 (p621) catalogs further named frailty instruments beyond FPP/FI/CFS/EFS — Gill Frailty Measure, Brief Frailty Instrument, Vulnerable Elders Survey (VES-13), FRAIL Scale (p621–622) Table 42-3 also spells out the CFS's 7 categories (p621): 1 = very fit; 2 = well (no active disease); 3 = well, with treated comorbid disease; 4 = apparently vulnerable (not frankly dependent, "slowed up"); 5 = mildly frail (IADL help only); 6 = moderately frail (help with IADLs + ADLs); 7 = severely frail (ADL-dependent) or terminally ill VES-13: frail if score ≥3 (range 0–10); FRAIL Scale (fatigue, resistance, ambulation, illness count >5, weight loss >5%): 0 = no frailty, 1–2 = intermediate, ≥3 = frailty (p622)
new: Table 42-3 (p621) catalogs further named frailty instruments beyond FPP/FI/CFS/EFS — Gill Frailty Measure, Brief Frailty Instrument, Vulnerable Elders Survey (VES-13), FRAIL Scale (p621–622) Table 42-3 also spells out the original CFS’s seven categories (p621): 1 = very fit; 2 = well (no active disease); 3 = well, with treated comorbid disease; 4 = apparently vulnerable (not frankly dependent, "slowed up"); 5 = mildly frail (IADL help only); 6 = moderately frail (help with IADLs + ADLs); 7 = severely frail (ADL-dependent) or terminally ill. The current nine-point CFS scores terminal illness as 9. VES-13: frail if score ≥3 (range 0–10); FRAIL Scale (fatigue, resistance, ambulation, ≥5 of 11 specified illnesses, weight loss ≥5% over the preceding year): 0 = no frailty, 1–2 = intermediate, ≥3 = frailty (p622; validated FRAIL questionnaire, Morley et al., PMCID PMC4515112).

old: Two large General-Practice-based trials (fractures n = 5451; serious fall injuries n = 9803) found NO significant reduction in falls or fractures — raises questions about funding/implementing interventions; multifactorial interventions work better when provided directly than when relying on referral to routine service providers (p641).
new: Two large primary-care trials found no significant reduction in their respective primary outcomes: fractures in PreFIT (9,803 participants) and serious fall injuries in STRIDE (5,451 participants). Direct delivery and uptake of the intervention may matter when implementing prevention through existing services (p641; PreFIT, STRIDE).

old: Diagnostic: AHI > 15 alone, or > 5 with symptoms/comorbidities; AHI > 30 = severe (p645).
new: Adult obstructive sleep apnea can be diagnosed with ≥15 obstructive respiratory events/hour, or ≥5/hour with relevant symptoms or comorbidities. Severe OSA begins at AHI ≥30/hour (p645; ICSD-3-TR, VA/DoD 2025 guideline, Appendix F).

old: ASV generally not recommended if EF less than 45% (SERVE-HF: increased mortality) (p649).
new: SERVE-HF found increased mortality with its ASV device in symptomatic chronic heart failure, LVEF ≤45% and predominantly central sleep apnea. Any consideration of ASV in HFrEF requires an experienced center, shared decision-making and close follow-up (p649; SERVE-HF, AASM 2025 central sleep apnea guideline).

old: PLMS last 0.5 seconds to 10 seconds, 5 to 90 seconds apart; at least four in a row required; PLMD needs at least 15 PLMS/hour (p651).
new: PLMS last 0.5–10 seconds, occur 5–90 seconds apart and comprise at least four consecutive movements. Adult PLMD requires more than 15 movements/hour with clinically significant sleep disturbance or daytime dysfunction unexplained by another disorder (p651; AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).

old: Start iron if ferritin less than 75 mcg/L; consider IV iron if ferritin less than 300 mcg/L with moderate-severe symptoms, although IV iron is usually reserved for iron malabsorption (p652).
new: Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in clinically significant RLS. AASM guidance considers iron at ferritin ≤75 µg/L or transferrin saturation <20%, with IV iron when ferritin is 75–100 µg/L if iron is indicated. The moderate–severe RLS trial permitting ferritin 75–300 µg/L required transferrin saturation <20% in that range (p652; trial, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).

old: Drugs (Table 44-2, p653): Ropinirole 0.25–4 mg, Pramipexole 0.125–2 mg — caution: augmentation, behavioral disinhibition. Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg — reserve for infrequent dosing (highest augmentation risk). Gabapentin enacarbil 600–1200 mg (only α2δ ligand FDA-approved for RLS), gabapentin 100–1800 mg, pregabalin 300 mg — caution: sedation, suicidal ideation. Clonazepam 0.25–2 mg, temazepam 15–30 mg — limited evidence, cognitive risk. Opiate agents (all off-label) for refractory RLS: codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg, methadone 5–10 mg.Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026; Current practice (not the book): AASM conditionally suggests against standard pramipexole, transdermal rotigotine or ropinirole use in adults with RLS because of augmentation with longer-term treatment; evidence certainty is moderate for pramipexole/ropinirole and low for rotigotine; patients prioritizing short-term symptom relief over long-term adverse effects may still choose these agents - AASM 2025, recommendations 12-14, p144
new: RLS drug selection. The AASM favors gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil and pregabalin when appropriate. FDA-labeled gabapentin enacarbil is 600 mg daily for RLS with normal renal function; 1,200 mg adds adverse effects without additional benefit. Dopamine agonists can cause augmentation and behavioral disinhibition. If pramipexole is chosen, the labeled RLS titration is 0.125–0.5 mg once daily. The labeled ropinirole range begins at 0.25 mg, up to 4 mg daily. Table 44-2 lists carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg for infrequent use because of augmentation. Table 44-2 lists off-label gabapentin 100–1,800 mg and pregabalin 300 mg as studied doses. Adjust for renal function and monitor sedation. The table lists clonazepam 0.25–2 mg and temazepam 15–30 mg, with limited evidence and cognitive/fall risks. Its off-label opioid examples are codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg and methadone 5–10 mg. These are historical table ranges. Specialist assessment of respiratory, dependence and medication risks is essential in refractory RLS (p653; FDA prescribing information for Horizant and pramipexole, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026; Current practice (not the book): AASM conditionally suggests against standard pramipexole, transdermal rotigotine or ropinirole use in adults with RLS because of augmentation with longer-term treatment; evidence certainty is moderate for pramipexole/ropinirole and low for rotigotine; patients prioritizing short-term symptom relief over long-term adverse effects may still choose these agents - AASM 2025, recommendations 12-14, p144

old: Tasimelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) approved only for non–24-hour sleep-wake rhythm disorder (p657).
new: Tasimelteon is an MT1/MT2 agonist approved for Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in adults and for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith–Magenis syndrome. The formulation for the latter depends on age (p657; FDA Hetlioz prescribing information).

old: Chronic if symptoms persist more than 3 months; short-term if fewer than 3 months (p657).
new: Chronic insomnia causes sleep difficulty despite adequate opportunity, with daytime consequences, at least 3 nights/week for at least 3 months. Short-term insomnia lasts less than 3 months (p657; ICSD-3-TR, VA/DoD 2025 guideline, Appendix F).

old: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Suvorexant/lemborexant (DORA) — only suvorexant FDA-approved for insomnia with Alzheimer dementia (trial of 277 patients, mild-moderate AD, sleep time up around half an hour after 2 weeks) (p660). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).
new: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Suvorexant and lemborexant are dual orexin receptor antagonists for insomnia. The suvorexant trial in mild–moderate probable Alzheimer dementia randomized 285, of whom 277 completed. Placebo-adjusted total sleep time improved by 28 minutes at week 4 (p660; Herring et al., FDA Belsomra prescribing information). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).

old: AHI greater than 15 is diagnostic alone (or greater than 5 with significant symptoms/comorbidities); AHI greater than 30 is severe (p645).
new: At least 15 obstructive respiratory events/hour suffice, or at least 5/hour with relevant symptoms or comorbidities. An AHI of 30/hour or more is severe (p645; ICSD-3-TR).

old: EF less than 45% — the SERVE-HF trial found increased mortality with ASV in this group (p649).
