old: LVRS candidates: FEV1 <50% predicted, RV >150–200% predicted, upper-lobe-predominant emphysema; FEV1 or DLCO <20% predicted + homogeneous emphysema = higher surgical mortality, do not operate (p1258).
new: LVRS candidates: FEV1 <50% predicted, RV >150–200% predicted, upper-lobe-predominant emphysema; For surgical risk, check the original NETT definition: FEV₁ at most 20% predicted, together with either homogeneous emphysema on CT or DLCO at most 20% predicted. This subgroup had excess operative mortality and little functional benefit. Page 1258 groups the criteria differently. NETT high-risk analysis.

old: FEV1 or DLCO < 20% predicted with homogeneous (rather than upper-lobe-predominant) emphysema — higher surgical mortality; should not undergo LVRS (p1258).
new: In NETT, FEV₁ at most 20% predicted plus either homogeneous emphysema or DLCO at most 20% predicted identified patients at high surgical risk. The 30-day mortality was 16% after surgery versus 0% with medical treatment. Page 1258 phrases the criteria differently. Original NETT analysis.

old: Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH, normal free T4/T3; prevalence 1-6%, persistence >50% on repeat testing. Treatment is now recommended (increased AF, heart failure, CV mortality, fracture, dementia risk) (p1551).
new: Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH, normal free T4/T3; prevalence 1-6%, persistence >50% on repeat testing. Confirm persistence. For adults aged 65 and older with endogenous subclinical hyperthyroidism, the ATA recommends treatment when TSH stays below 0.1 mU/L, and consideration of treatment when it remains between 0.1 mU/L and the lower reference limit. Consider symptoms, cardiac disease and osteoporosis (p1551). ATA recommendations 83 and 85.

old: Myxedema coma: give IV hydrocortisone before/with thyroid hormone — treating with thyroid hormone alone can precipitate adrenal crisis. Initial levothyroxine 200-400 μg, then 75-100 μg/day; avoid added T3 (cardiac risk) (p1553).
new: Myxedema coma: give IV hydrocortisone before/with thyroid hormone — treating with thyroid hormone alone can precipitate adrenal crisis. Initial IV levothyroxine 200–400 μg, using the lower end for older patients or those with cardiac disease, then the chapter gives 75–100 μg/day. Rapid T3 exposure may increase cardiac risk (p1553; ATA recommendation 21a).

old: Table 87-9 laxative mechanisms (owner-highlighted): sodium picosulfate is hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria, bisacodyl by intestinal/colonic brush-border enzymes — both to the same active metabolite (antiabsorptive/secretory, prokinetic); sorbitol/lactulose are nonabsorbable disaccharides metabolized by colonic bacteria to short-chain fatty acids; PEG osmotically increases intraluminal fluids; senna/anthraquinones alter electrolyte transport via increased intraluminal fluids, stimulate the myenteric plexus, and increase motility (p1373–1374).
new: Table 87-9 laxative mechanisms (owner-highlighted): sodium picosulfate is hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria, bisacodyl by intestinal/colonic brush-border enzymes — both to the same active metabolite (antiabsorptive/secretory, prokinetic); lactulose is a nonabsorbed disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria, while sorbitol is an osmotic sugar alcohol; PEG osmotically increases intraluminal fluids; senna/anthraquinones alter electrolyte transport via increased intraluminal fluids, stimulate the myenteric plexus, and increase motility (p1373–1374).

old: Diabetes: colonic transit prolongs to 200 ± 144 h in immobile diabetics. If using metoclopramide, older adults should avoid continuous treatment for longer than 12 weeks, with a 2-week drug holiday or a dose decrease as tolerated (tardive dyskinesia risk) (p1361).
new: Diabetes: colonic transit prolongs to 200 ± 144 h in immobile diabetics. Metoclopramide may treat diabetic gastroparesis. Tardive dyskinesia risk rises with total exposure. For diabetic gastroparesis, US prescribing information advises avoiding more than 12 weeks of total treatment. A drug holiday does not reset cumulative exposure (p1361). Reglan prescribing information, Boxed Warning

old: PAMORAs for opioid-induced constipation — naldemedine (52% vs 35% achieving >3 CSBM vs placebo) and naloxegol (42% vs 29% achieving ≥3 CSBM/wk) (p1378).
new: PAMORAs for opioid-induced constipation — naldemedine and naloxegol counter opioid effects in the gut. Pooled response rates on p1378 are 52% vs 35% and 42% vs 29%, respectively. The pivotal trials measured spontaneous bowel movements, without requiring a sense of complete evacuation. Responders had at least three per week and at least one more than baseline for nine of twelve weeks, including three of the last four. COMPOSE trials · KODIAC trials

old: Why must metoclopramide use in older adults be time-limited, and beyond what duration should continuous treatment be avoided?

old: Risk of tardive dyskinesia is increased in older adults; avoid continuous treatment for longer than 12 weeks.
new: Older adults are particularly susceptible to tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. For diabetic gastroparesis, avoid more than 12 weeks of total treatment.

old: A 2-week drug holiday or a decrease of metoclopramide dose as tolerated (with tight blood glucose control) is encouraged whenever clinically possible (p1361).
new: Interrupting treatment or reducing the dose does not erase previous exposure (p1361 and the Reglan boxed warning above).

old: Up to 90% of RBD patients develop a synucleinopathy (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia, MSA) over 10- to 15-year follow-up (p654).
new: In selected longitudinal cohorts, up to 90% of people presenting with isolated RBD developed a clinically evident synucleinopathy (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia, MSA) over 10- to 15-year follow-up (p654).

old: Below what ejection fraction is adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) generally not recommended for central sleep apnea, and why?
new: Which heart-failure population had excess mortality with the ASV device in SERVE-HF, and how does this inform referral?

old: LVEF ≤45% in symptomatic chronic heart failure with predominantly central sleep apnea. SERVE-HF found higher mortality with its ASV device in this population (p649; PMID 26323938).
new: LVEF ≤45% in symptomatic chronic heart failure with predominantly central sleep apnea. SERVE-HF found higher mortality with its ASV device in this population. The AASM limits consideration of ASV for central apnea in HFrEF to experienced centers with shared decision-making and close follow-up (p649). AASM 2025, recommendation 4

old: What proportion of REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) patients go on to develop a synucleinopathy, and over what time frame?
new: What long-term risk of a clinically evident synucleinopathy has been described in selected cohorts presenting with isolated RBD?

old: Up to 90%, over 10 to 15 years of follow-up (p654).
new: Up to 90% over 10 to 15 years in selected clinical cohorts. This estimate applies to isolated RBD and is not an individual prediction (p654, Figure 44-8).

old: CGA-guided intervention RCTs reduce treatment toxicity: cluster RCT across 41 practices, 718 patients → 20% absolute reduction in toxicity vs usual care; single-center MDT-CGA RCT in 620 patients → 10% reduction in chemo toxicity (p1388).
new: Geriatric assessment reduced severe toxicity in two trials: in GAP70+ it fell from 71% to 51% with tailored recommendations for the oncologist, and in GAIN it fell from 60.6% to 50.5% with multidisciplinary implementation (p1388).

old: Telomere shortening begins at age 30 and proceeds at ~1%/year loss; loss of telomere function → genetic instability → oncogenic mutation risk (p1383).
new: Telomeres protect chromosome ends. Their progressive loss can destabilize chromosomes and increase mutation risk. Page 1383 describes a functional decline from age 30 at about 1% per year. Measured leukocyte telomere shortening also occurs in infancy, and its rate varies with age. Human leukocyte study

old: ECOG performance status (0 = perfect health, 5 = death) alone is not sufficient in geriatric oncology — a comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) adds substantial prognostic/functional information even in patients with a good ECOG PS (p1387–1388).
new: ECOG performance status (0 = fully active without restriction from disease, 5 = death) alone is not sufficient in geriatric oncology — a comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) adds substantial prognostic/functional information even in patients with a good ECOG PS (p1387–1388).

old: Surgery: healing is compromised at every phase (↓inflammatory/proliferative response, altered collagen); geriatric comanagement improves 90-day postoperative mortality (p1388–1389).
new: Surgery: healing is compromised at every phase (↓inflammatory/proliferative response, altered collagen); in a retrospective cohort of patients aged 75 or older undergoing cancer surgery, geriatric comanagement was associated with lower 90-day mortality (pp1388–1389). Original surgical cohort

old: Immunotherapy (ICIs): equivalent incidence of high-grade irAEs in older vs younger adults, but worse overall survival among older adults who develop high-grade irAEs — likely because steroids/hospitalization for irAE treatment are less well tolerated (p1391).
new: Immunotherapy (ICIs): one retrospective cohort observed similar frequencies of high-grade immune-related events by age. Among those with high-grade events, the older group had shorter median survival. Susceptibility to complications of steroids or hospitalization is one proposed explanation (p1391). Original cohort, Table 3

old: Routine symptom assessment/intervention can improve overall survival upwards of 5 months with no change in cancer-directed treatment (p1391).
new: In one trial of electronic symptom monitoring during treatment, median survival was 31.2 versus 26.0 months. A later community trial found better symptom control, function and quality of life without a survival difference. Symptom monitoring can help even when survival is unchanged (p1391). Original trial · PRO-TECT

old: End-of-life nutrition: IV fluids/TPN/tube feeding do not prolong life and may worsen comfort (pulmonary congestion, edema); dehydration near death is generally comfortable except for xerostomia (treat with swabs/ice chips) (p1392).
new: In the last days of life with advanced cancer, routine artificial hydration or nutrition has no established survival benefit and can add edema, pulmonary congestion or procedural burden. Ask about thirst and discomfort, offer mouth care and safe sips or ice chips as tolerated, and individualize decisions with the patient and family (p1392). NCI, Last Days of Life

new: How can loss of telomere function promote malignancy, and when has telomere shortening been measured?

old: Begins at age 30, progressing at a loss of approximately 1% per year (p1383).
new: Loss of chromosome-end protection can promote genomic instability. The chapter describes functional decline from age 30 at about 1% per year (p1383). Leukocyte measurements show that shortening is already present in early childhood and proceeds at an age-dependent rate.

new: Cachexia: severe weight loss and wasting in cancer, HIV infection, or end-stage organ failure. Low muscle mass overlaps with sarcopenia, but excess catabolism/inflammation and endocrine/neurologic changes differ. Identify the underlying disease and its catabolic effects. Nutrition and exercise may support function when feasible, but these measures alone cannot fully reverse disease-driven wasting (p736).

old: DOACs preferred over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for nonvalvular AF — valvular AF (moderate–severe MS or mechanical valve) needs warfarin regardless of score; no dabigatran/rivaroxaban/edoxaban in ESRD/dialysis (Table 77-8, p1203); apixaban and edoxaban show lower major-bleeding risk in patients 75 years or older (p1202), while full-dose dabigatran and rivaroxaban carry increased GI bleeding risk (PPI recommended).
new: DOACs preferred over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for nonvalvular AF — valvular AF (moderate–severe MS or mechanical valve) needs warfarin regardless of score; no dabigatran/rivaroxaban/edoxaban in ESRD/dialysis (Table 77-8, p1203); apixaban and edoxaban show lower major-bleeding risk in patients 75 years or older (p1202), while full-dose dabigatran and rivaroxaban carry increased GI bleeding risk (p1202 recommends a PPI with these agents). In clinical practice, individualize gastroprotection according to overall gastrointestinal bleeding risk. ESC 2024 AF guideline, §6.7.1.

old: Apixaban and edoxaban show lower major bleeding; full-dose dabigatran and rivaroxaban are associated with increased GI bleeding risk (a PPI is recommended with these two) (p1202).
new: Apixaban and edoxaban show lower major bleeding; full-dose dabigatran and rivaroxaban are associated with increased GI bleeding risk (p1202). Hazzard recommends a PPI with these agents. The 2024 ESC guideline individualizes gastroprotection according to gastrointestinal bleeding risk.

old: ~240 million worldwide have symptomatic OA; ≥32 million in the US. OA is the 3rd leading cause of years lived with disability in the US and the most common cause of mobility limitation in older adults (p779).
new: The chapter estimates ~240 million people worldwide with symptomatic OA and ≥32 million in the US. In the data it cites, OA ranked third for years lived with disability in the US and was the most common cause of mobility limitation in older adults (p779).

old: Genetics: 90 genome-wide significant OA risk loci identified; COL2A1 (type II collagen) is among the implicated genes (p780).
new: Genetics: 90 genome-wide significant OA risk loci reported in the studies available to the chapter; COL2A1 (type II collagen) is among the implicated genes (p780).

old: Viscosupplementation (IA hyaluronic acid): not recommended by ACR/AF/OARSI (p789). Platelet-rich plasma/mesenchymal stem cell therapy: still experimental and not FDA-approved — only within an FDA-approved trial (p789); ACR/AF strongly against for knee/hip (Figure 52-5, p786).
new: Viscosupplementation (intra-articular hyaluronic acid) has little clear benefit in low-bias trials. ACR/AF recommends against it for knee OA, while OARSI allows selected knee use depending on comorbidities (p789 and the guideline comparison above). Hazzard advises restricting PRP and mesenchymal stem-cell treatments to trials (p789). ACR/AF recommends against both for knee and hip OA. For symptomatic knee OA specifically, AAOS gives limited support to PRP for pain and function because trial results vary. These treatments have not been shown to restore lost cartilage. AAOS knee OA guideline, Platelet-rich Plasma.

old: At least 32 million people (out of ~240 million worldwide with symptomatic OA); OA is the 3rd leading cause of years lived with disability in the US (p779).
new: The chapter reports at least 32 million people in the US and about 240 million worldwide. OA ranked third for years lived with disability in the US estimates it cites (p779).

old: Glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate (no more effective than placebo in the lowest-bias data), TNF inhibitors and IL-1 receptor antagonists (not efficacious for erosive OA), and bisphosphonates (no efficacy for pain or function) (p788; Figure 52-5, p786).
new: Glucosamine for hand, hip or knee OA, and chondroitin sulfate for hip or knee OA. Hand OA is an exception: ACR/AF conditionally recommends chondroitin sulfate for this site. Other drugs recommended against include TNF inhibitors and IL-1 receptor antagonists (not efficacious for erosive OA), and bisphosphonates (no efficacy for pain or function) (p788; Figure 52-5, p786).

old: Clozapine 6.25–75 mg/day — low EPS risk, so a good option for psychotic symptoms in DLB (DLB/PD patients are extremely EPS-sensitive, except to clozapine); limited by neutropenia/agranulocytosis — weekly blood draws in the first 6 months (p928).
new: Clozapine 6.25–75 mg/day — lower motor risk than potent dopamine blockers, but it can still cause serious harm. Evidence of benefit comes from Parkinson disease psychosis. Efficacy and tolerability specifically in DLB remain uncertain. Seek specialist input if persistent dangerous or severely distressing psychosis warrants a trial. DLB Consortium consensus. Use is limited by neutropenia/agranulocytosis — weekly blood draws in the first 6 months (p928).

old: Escitalopram — the cleaner S-enantiomer of citalopram; being studied for agitation (S-CitAD) (p930).
new: Escitalopram — the S-enantiomer of citalopram. S-CitAD, ongoing when p930 was written, later found no significant benefit for agitation at 12 weeks. S-CitAD trial.

old: Mirtazapine — sedating at lower doses; in one RCT (24 vs 16) no benefit over placebo for sleep in dementia, with increased daytime sleepiness (p930).
new: Mirtazapine — sedating at lower doses; in the sleep pilot, 8 received mirtazapine and 16 placebo (24 total). Nighttime sleep did not improve and daytime sleepiness increased. Page 930 misstates the treatment-group size. Scoralick et al., methods and results.

old: Which antipsychotic's low EPS risk makes it a good option for psychotic symptoms in dementia with Lewy bodies, and what limits its use?

old: Clozapine — limited by serious adverse effects (neutropenia/agranulocytosis) and close laboratory monitoring: weekly blood draws in the first 6 months (p928).
new: Clozapine has lower motor toxicity, but efficacy and tolerability in dementia with Lewy bodies are uncertain. Neutropenia can be life-threatening and requires absolute neutrophil count monitoring, typically weekly in the first six months (p928).

old: Culture stewardship: almost universally, do NOT culture skin-surface swabs or urine in the presence of a long-term indwelling catheter — such cultures will always be positive but don't correlate with infection, are more often misleading than helpful, and should NOT guide antibiotic selection (KCP #3, p1668; reinforced p1671). old: Several small studies estimate 18F-FDG uptake in the temporal, maxillary, or vertebral arteries occurs in 64–82% of GCA patients, with very high specificity; some authors conclude temporal artery biopsy may be avoided when cranial-artery uptake is absent — corticosteroids for more than a few days can markedly reduce the sensitivity of both PET/CT and biopsy (p1676)
new: Several small studies estimate 18F-FDG uptake in the temporal, maxillary, or vertebral arteries occurs in 64–82% of GCA patients, with very high specificity; those historical studies do not support ruling out GCA from a negative cranial PET alone. With persistent suspicion, investigate further. Do not delay treatment when clinical suspicion is strong, particularly with threatened vision (p1676; EULAR, principles A and C)

new: Compatible new symptoms justify a urine culture before treatment when feasible, even without sepsis. Culture the fresh catheter if replaced (pp1668, 1671, 1673).

old: Compare TST and IFGRA sensitivity for latent TB in older adults, and state which is now used for most latent TB testing and why.
new: Which test for TB infection is preferred after BCG vaccination, and what is the limit of a positive result?

old: TST ~70% vs IFGRA ~75% (IFGRA only minimally more sensitive); most latent TB testing is now done by IFGRA because it needs only a single blood draw (no return visit), doesn't need two-step testing in nursing home residents, and has greater interrater reliability and specificity (p1675).
new: IGRA is preferred after BCG because the vaccine does not cause a positive blood test. It requires one blood draw. A positive IGRA or skin test warrants assessment for active TB before diagnosing latent infection (p1675).

new: For initial nonfulminant CDI, IDSA/SHEA favors fidaxomicin when feasible; oral vancomycin remains an acceptable alternative; metronidazole is not first-line monotherapy (p1672); for fulminant CDI, combine enteral vancomycin and IV metronidazole, especially with ileus (p1673); a study of patients with recent CDI needing other antibiotics reported recurrence of 4% with oral vancomycin prophylaxis versus 26% without it; this was a historical study result. old: Cognitive screening at diagnosis, then annually if borderline or every 2–3 years if normal (p1568).
new: The chapter gives annual follow-up after a borderline cognitive screen and every 2–3 years after a normal screen (p1568). ADA 2026 recommends an initial screen and annual screening from age 65, with additional assessment when self-management changes.

old: BP target <140/90 mmHg for most; consider 130/80 mmHg for high-risk (prior stroke, progressing CKD), with orthostatic monitoring (p1572).
new: Hazzard gives a BP goal below 140/90 mmHg for most (p1572). ADA 2026 recommends below 130/80 mmHg when safely attainable. For poor health, limited life expectancy or high treatment risk, a goal such as below 140/90 may be appropriate. Check standing BP (ADA 2026, recommendation 13.9).

old: Benzodiazepines (eg clonazepam) for neuropathic pain: daily use >30 days risks physiologic dependence — taper, don't stop abruptly; tracked as lorazepam milligram equivalents (LMEs) in PDMPs (p1065)
new: Regular benzodiazepine use can cause physical dependence within days to weeks. The book highlights daily use beyond 30 days. When stopping a drug such as clonazepam in a physically dependent patient, taper gradually. Some prescription monitoring programs track lorazepam milligram equivalents (p1065, FDA boxed warning).

old: Daily use for more than 30 days can cause physical dependence, so reduce gradually if stopping.
new: Physical dependence can develop within days to weeks of regular use, even at prescribed doses. When dependence is likely, taper gradually and adjust the pace to withdrawal symptoms (FDA boxed warning on benzodiazepines).

old: After how many days of daily benzodiazepine use can older adults develop physiologic dependence, and how should the drug be stopped?
new: How soon can regular benzodiazepine use cause physical dependence, and how should the drug be stopped if dependence is likely?

old: More than 30 days of daily use; the drug should be gradually tapered rather than stopped abruptly, to avoid withdrawal (p1065).
new: Physical dependence can begin within days to weeks. Page 1065 highlights risk after 30 days of daily treatment. Individualize a gradual taper when dependence is likely because abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures (FDA boxed warning).

old: Full replacement dose in older adults is lower than the young-adult 1.6 μg/kg/day; "start low, go slow" in patients ≥65 with cardiac disease, using 25-50 μg tablets (p1552).
new: Full replacement dose in older adults is lower than the young-adult 1.6 μg/kg/day. With known coronary artery disease, start oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 μg/day and increase cautiously according to symptoms and TSH (p1552, ATA section 4b).

old: Benign-nodule follow-up: repeat ultrasound in 12-18 months, then surveillance every 2-5 years. A nodule with two benign FNAs needs no further aspiration (p1556).
new: After a benign FNA, match surveillance to ultrasound risk. High suspicion calls for repeat ultrasound and US-guided FNA within 12 months. Low or intermediate suspicion calls for ultrasound at 12–24 months. With very low suspicion, wait at least 24 months if rescanning. Two benign US-guided FNAs end routine surveillance for malignancy in that nodule (p1556, ATA recommendation 23).

old: The chapter cites 25–50 micrograms as reasonable starting doses.
new: The chapter gives 25–50 micrograms as examples. For stable primary hypothyroidism with known coronary artery disease, the ATA advises starting oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 micrograms daily and titrating to symptoms and TSH (ATA, section 4b).

old: After a benign aspirate, repeat ultrasound initially at 12–18 months.
new: After a first benign aspirate, page 1556 gives an initial ultrasound interval of 12–18 months. ATA recommendation 23 uses the ultrasound pattern. A highly suspicious nodule needs repeat ultrasound and US-guided aspiration within 12 months. For low or intermediate suspicion, repeat ultrasound at 12–24 months. For very low suspicion, any repeat scan should be at least 24 months later.

old: With two benign aspirates the likelihood of two false negatives is very low.
new: After two benign US-guided aspirates, cancer surveillance of that nodule can stop. A large nodule may still need review if it causes pressure symptoms (ATA, recommendation 23).

old: "Start low, go slow" using the smallest tablets (25-50 μg).
new: For stable primary hypothyroidism with known coronary artery disease, start oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 μg daily and titrate gradually according to cardiac symptoms and TSH (ATA section 4b).

old: 500 pg/mL is highly suggestive of active HF; <100 pg/mL makes HF much less likely.
new: A BNP above 500 pg/mL strongly supports active heart failure in the appropriate clinical context. A BNP below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure much less likely in a nonobese older adult.

old: A population-based study recorded clinical seizures within 24 hours in 8.4% of hemorrhagic and 2.4% of ischemic strokes.
new: Within 24 hours of onset, 8.4% of patients with hemorrhagic stroke and 2.9% of those with cerebral infarction had a seizure. Pooling infarction with transient ischemic attack lowered the latter figure to 2.4%.

old: Routine primary antiseizure prophylaxis after spontaneous ICH is generally unnecessary (p976, Harrison 21e p3310, Szaflarski et al., Epilepsia 2008, 49:974–981).
new: Routine primary antiseizure prophylaxis after spontaneous ICH is generally unnecessary (p976, Harrison 21e p3310, Szaflarski et al., Table 2).

old: Low-dose rapamycin/mTOR inhibition, senolytics and metformin are discussed as research approaches; the chapter does not establish routine anti-aging prescriptions (p60, p62).
new: The influenza vaccine study used everolimus (RAD001), a rapamycin derivative that inhibits mTOR. It measured antibody responses in older adults. The separate rapamycin longevity experiments were in mice. These findings support research into mTOR biology; they do not provide a clinical indication to prescribe an anti-aging treatment (pp. 60, 62). Original human trial.
